PIT and randomised quantile residuals

Source: R/gamm4-methods.R, R/gjrm-diagnostics.R, R/mixed-diagnostics.R, and 2 more
quantile_residuals.Rd

Map observations to probabilities under the fitted response distribution. These probability integral transform (PIT) residuals have a uniform reference distribution under a correctly specified continuous model with known parameters. Quantile residuals transform them to standard-normal scores. Discrete observations require randomisation over their probability mass.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'gamm4'
quantile_residuals(
  model,
  type = c("pit", "quantile"),
  seed = NULL,
  conditioning = NULL,
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'gamlss'
quantile_residuals(model, type = c("pit", "quantile"), seed = NULL, ...)

# S3 method for class 'gamm'
quantile_residuals(
  model,
  type = c("pit", "quantile"),
  seed = NULL,
  conditioning = NULL,
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'gratia_diagnostic_proxy'
quantile_residuals(
  model,
  type = c("pit", "quantile"),
  seed = NULL,
  conditioning = NULL,
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'lme'
quantile_residuals(
  model,
  type = c("pit", "quantile"),
  seed = NULL,
  conditioning = NULL,
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'merMod'
quantile_residuals(
  model,
  type = c("pit", "quantile"),
  seed = NULL,
  conditioning = NULL,
  ...
)

quantile_residuals(model, type = c("pit", "quantile"), seed = NULL, ...)

# S3 method for class 'gam'
quantile_residuals(

# S3 method for class 'glm'

# S3 method for class 'lm'
quantile_residuals(model, type = c("pit", "quantile"), seed = NULL, ...)

# Default S3 method
quantile_residuals(

  type = c("pit", "quantile"),
  seed = NULL,

  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'glmmTMB'
quantile_residuals(

  conditioning = NULL,
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'gratia_glmmtmb_diagnostic'
quantile_residuals(
  model,
  type = c("pit", "quantile"),
  seed = NULL,
  conditioning = NULL,
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'sdmTMB'
quantile_residuals(
  model,
  type = c("pit", "quantile"),
  seed = NULL,
  conditioning = NULL,
  component = "response",
  field_method = c("mle-mvn", "mle-eb", "mle-mvn-integrated"),
  ...
)

Arguments

model

a fitted model object.

type

character; "pit" returns probabilities and "quantile" returns standard-normal scores.

seed

integer or NULL; random seed for randomised residuals. With NULL, calculations use the current random-number state. An explicit seed preserves the caller's state, including when none was previously initialised.

conditioning

character or NULL; hold fitted random effects fixed ("conditional"), average over new effects ("marginal"), or use the extracted GAM ("gam_component"), where supported. See diagnostic_support.

...

arguments passed to other methods.

component

character; which delta sdmTMB component to check; see appraise().

field_method

For sdmTMB diagnostics, "mle-mvn" (the default) follows sdmTMB's recommended residual calculation. Draw the fitted random effects together once from their approximate posterior, then use that same draw to evaluate the response CDF and generate every reference response. Fixed coefficients and covariance parameters remain at their maximum likelihood estimates. The independent seed in gratia.diagnostics.field_seed (default

  1. keeps different diagnostic panels on the same draw of the effects. "mle-eb" uses the fitted empirical-Bayes effects without drawing their uncertainty; sdmTMB does not recommend this mode for goodness-of-fit testing. "mle-mvn-integrated" draws new values of the fitted effects for each simulation, from their approximate posterior. Residuals use the rank of each response among the simulated reference responses. This averages over uncertainty in the fitted effects, but reuses the data used in fitting and can make goodness-of-fit checks less likely to detect departures. These residuals differ from sdmTMB's calculation at a single draw of the effects. With conditioning = "marginal", new spatial, temporal and group effects are drawn from their fitted prior distributions, while smooth effects remain at fitted values; field_method does not add another draw of the fields. These approximations do not guarantee that goodness-of-fit tests have their intended false-positive rate after parameter estimation. Posterior predictive checks separately include coefficient and field uncertainty, as described in their plot subtitle. Student-t responses use the fitted location, scale and fixed or estimated degrees of freedom. The scale is not the response standard deviation. Pearson residuals require degrees of freedom greater than two, because their response variance is otherwise infinite. PIT, quantile residuals and posterior predictive checks remain available when this variance is infinite.

Details

With na.exclude, excluded observations are restored as NA residuals; with na.omit, only observations used for fitting are returned.

For mgcv::cnorm(), mgcv::clog() and mgcv::cpois() models, censored observations have PIT residuals sampled uniformly between F(l) and F(u). Here l and u bound the censoring interval and F is the fitted cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the underlying response. Left and right censoring use probabilities zero and one for the unbounded end, respectively. Quantile residuals apply qnorm() to these PIT values. Uncensored continuous observations use F(y); uncensored Poisson observations are randomised between F(y - 1) and F(y). Use non-integer censoring limits for cpois(), as recommended by mgcv.

For grouped-family GAMs fitted with mgcv::gfam(), each observation uses its component's CDF, fitted nuisance parameters, dispersion and weights. Residuals are returned in fitting order. All active components must supply supported CDFs and probability limits for discrete or censored observations. Unsupported components give an error; appraise() can instead select deviance residuals automatically. See appraise() for supported families. Tweedie zeros have positive probability mass: their PITs are randomised between F(0-) = 0 and F(0). Positive observations use F(y).

When a CDF can calculate log probabilities in both tails, quantile residuals use the log probability in the smaller tail directly. This avoids infinities caused by rounding probabilities to zero or one. Probabilities are not clipped, so true zero-probability tails still give infinite residuals for ordinary models; grouped diagnostics report non-finite residuals as errors. PITs are returned as ordinary probabilities and may still round to zero or one in extreme tails. Applying qnorm() to returned PITs can therefore be less accurate than requesting quantile residuals directly. CDFs without log probabilities retain ordinary-probability calculations.

Marginal checks may calculate residuals from ranks in joint response simulations when no analytic marginal CDF is available. See diagnostic_support for the rank definition, conditioning choices and limitations after fitting.
